As to the title, I'm not sure about every major population center, but I would be surprised if there have not been small devices in certain key cities around the world. Cloak and dagger shenanigans require daggers, after all, otherwise it's just people playing dress-up. Whether they would still present or even functional is another matter. Anything you don't have total control over is something that can be intercepted, sabotaged, removed, or broken. An ICBM in your own country is easier to keep working than something hidden away somewhere in "the enemy's" backyard.

Getting to the meat of the question, the "knowledge" for a basic device is frighteningly simple, so much so that the "Little Boy" device dropped on Hiroshima wasn't even tested first. It wasn't the strongest, it wasn't the most efficient, but the scientists working on it knew academically that it would function. The first device tested was of a "Fat Man" design, which was far more complex, and so they weren't sure it would actually work as intended. There is no way to regulate the knowledge because it stems from the nature of nuclear physics itself. If you understand the "why" well enough, you can eventually work out the "how" if you have the resources available. Dissemination of the actual processes involved (from someone such as Dr. Khan, the Pakistani nuclear scientist who sold the information to whomever could pay) saves time, effort, and money as it cuts down on the trial and error of dialing things in. You could figure out how to bake a cake without a recipe, but it's a lot easier if you have a cookbook and don't have to reinvent the wheel.

The UN attempts to limit nuclear proliferation, but "information wants to be free," and it's extremely difficult to keep motivated parties from buying or stealing the knowledge, and impossible to stop them from just figuring out on their own short of direct action (kidnapping, sabotage, murder, etc.). This is part of the reason the US has had such a raging diplomatic hard-on about nuclear programs in non-friendly countries. Sure, the Iranians might not cook one off on us, but who's to say they won't sell one to someone who's willing to, and then act shocked when it happens. It's the same reason the US is so concerned about Pakistan and India. They both have nuclear arsenals, they both hate each other, and they're both teetering on the brink of collapse. Even if there's no nuclear war between the two, if either state collapses, who's going to maintain control and security of their weapons?

The limitations to a nuclear arsenal are mostly monetary, as they are very expensive to both create and maintain. The isotopes required to produce an effective device are not cheap to create or refine, and the more complex the device, the more expensive it is to produce and maintain. Delivery systems are also expensive, but that's another topic.

The only thing stopping Ireland from deciding it wants nukes is essentially the lack of desire. The South Africans were apparently concerned about a potential Soviet invasion, as Angolan communists were being directly supported by Soviet and Cuban forces during their civil war. They designed and built a handful of small yield, tactical devices as a result. When the Soviets pulled out, the South Africans, already mostly cut off from the global economy due to sanctions over Apartheid, scrapped both the weapons and weapons program as they felt the money would be better suited elsewhere.

There are no "dark" secrets about them, the horrors are fairly self evident, and so they tend to be tightly controlled.
